    #171781. How to Prune a Christmas Tree – Fix a Too-Tall, Too-Wide, or Lopsided Tree for the Perfect Shape

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2275 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Prune a Christmas Tree – Fix a Too-Tall, Too-Wide, or Lopsided Tree for the Perfect Shape

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2275 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Unless you’re willing to settle for an artificial Christmas tree, you’re unlikely to find one that’s perfectly symmetrical.
    • Industry observers note that all of the best Christmas tree care in the world won’t help with these shaping issues.
    • Of course, knowing how to pick a Christmas tree with a good natural shape can save you some work in the first place.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Unless you’re willing to settle for an artificial Christmas tree, you’re unlikely to find one that’s perfectly symmetrical. We've all been there: you choose one that looks promising at the lot, then get it home and discover it's too tall or wide for your living room – or simply looks much more awkwardly shaped than you remembered. It’s enough to make you open the bottle of sherry you left out for Santa.

    Industry observers note that all of the best Christmas tree care in the world won’t help with these shaping issues. But a little careful pruning can make a big difference. Here, we will explain the steps to trim a too-tall, too-wide, or lopsided Christmas tree into a balanced, attractive centerpiece. We’ll also lay out the tools you need and the techniques you should use.

    Of course, knowing how to pick a Christmas tree with a good natural shape can save you some work in the first place. Before you begin trimming, remember that removing branches is much easier than putting them back. Work gradually, and try repositioning or fluffing branches before reaching for your pruners.

    A beautifully shaped Christmas tree should have a straight central trunk, a strong top branch to support a star or angel, and evenly spaced branches that create a full, balanced appearance.

    Commercial Christmas tree growers tend to encourage the classic conical Christmas tree shape through occasional pruning. They aim for a base width of around 60 to 70 percent of the tree's height, although a slimmer tree may be more practical for smaller rooms.

    It has been revealed that branch density matters, too. Large gaps between branch tiers can make a tree look sparse, while more closely spaced tiers create a fuller appearance – though denser branch tiers mean less space to hang ornaments.

    Industry observers note that the first step, once you bring the new tree into your home, is to make a fresh, straight cut about half an inch (1.3 cm) from the base of the trunk. Some sellers will do this for you before you load it into your car, but it needs to be fresh. If you're doing it yourself, a pruning saw, like Fiskars' Pro 10-Inch Pruning Saw, available on Amazon, will make the job easier. Then, put the tree straight into a sturdy container of water. This is one of the most important steps to make your Christmas tree last longer and prevent premature needle drop.

    Let the tree settle before doing any further trimming. Give the tree a few hours, or ideally overnight, to relax its branches. This is particularly important if the tree has been tightly wrapped in netting. Its branches need time to spread back into their natural positions, and what initially looks like an awkward gap or uneven section may become much less noticeable.

    Once the branches have relaxed, walk around the tree and look at it from several angles. Identify any protruding branches, bare patches, or uneven growth before deciding what actually needs cutting.

    According to recent reports, you’ll need clean, sharp tools to prune a real Christmas tree into a pleasing cone shape. With the right tools and techniques, you can create a full, appealing tree no matter how tall, wide, or wonky it started out.

    You can buy a hundred different tools for pruning trees, but you really don’t need more than a handful to prune a real Christmas tree. For smaller branches, a pair of budget-friendly pruners, like Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears, will give you the control needed to make clean, precise cuts. For thicker branches, use loppers, like Corona ComfortGEL Bypass Loppers, which provide extra cutting power.

    According to recent reports, for cutting through the trunk, use a sharp pruning saw or handsaw. Make sure the cut is straight so the tree sits securely in its stand.

    Is your Christmas tree too tall for your space? That’s usually one of the easiest Christmas tree problems to deal with, so don’t fret. First, measure your ceiling height, then subtract the height you need for the tree stand and tree topper, plus at least 1–2 inches (2.5–5 cm) of clearance. This is the perfect height for your latest tree. Then measure the tree to see how much you need to remove.

    Sources indicate that if you only need a modest reduction (say, a few inches), cut the excess length from the bottom of the trunk. Just make sure enough bare trunk remains to fit securely into the stand without forcing the lower branches against its rim. Then put the tree into its stand – ideally one with a built-in water reservoir, like the Krinner Genie Christmas Tree Stand.

    Industry observers note that if your tree is significantly too tall, removing a large section of the trunk could also mean losing its attractive lower branches. In this case, you may need to shorten the central leader at the top instead. This is the upright shoot that forms the tree's tip.

    Sometimes the leader is disproportionately tall and can easily be shortened without spoiling the tree's shape. Other times, cutting off the original tip can ruin its natural outline and remove the little knobbly buds and side shoots that help hold a tree topper in place. Indeed, it might be better to go without a topper rather than making a drastic cut. So treat trimming the tip of your Christmas tree as a last resort, and only if you think it will work with its natural shape.

    Recent findings suggest that if you do decide to take this step, trim the leader carefully to the desired height. Then assess the tree's upcoming shape and, if necessary, selectively shorten the surrounding branches until you achieve a symmetrical, conical outline. Work gradually, stepping back regularly to check your progress.

    When a tree is too wide to fit gracefully in your home, you can trim its branches. A traditionally shaped Christmas tree has a base width of around two-thirds its height. But it’s a good idea to measure the floor space where the tree will stand to make sure that the “ideal” shape will work for you.

    Start by positioning the tree where you want it to stand and turning it to find the most attractive side. If branches at the back prevent it from fitting neatly against the wall, trim these first. Then, look at the tree from the front and sides, shortening any branches that stick out too far or spoil its overall shape.

    In a recent development, work gradually, removing a little at a time, and step back often to check the results. You don't need to trim every branch to the same length – the aim is to create a balanced, natural-looking tree that fits comfortably in its space.

    For branches that genuinely need shortening, make cuts within the green, needle-covered portion of the growth. Avoid cutting too deeply into the bare, woody sections, as this can leave obvious gaps in the foliage that won't fill out.

    According to recent reports, remember that different types of Christmas trees naturally have different shapes. Some firs have a dense, compact outline, while certain spruces and pines have more open branching. Work with the tree's natural form rather than trying to force every variety into exactly the same silhouette.

    It’s easier to talk about a too-tall or too-wide Christmas tree than one that’s just kind of weird. Whether it's lopsided or just plain wonky, you can still improve that uneven Christmas tree shape to make it presentable.

    First, check that the trunk is standing straight in its base. Sometimes a tree that looks lopsided simply needs adjusting in the stand rather than pruning.

    To shape a lopsided Christmas tree, keep a cone shape in the front of your mind. Prune the upper branches shorter than the lower ones, and remember that the base width should be about two-thirds the tree's height. To achieve these goals, keep stepping back to see how things look.

    Industry observers note that take off any dead or damaged branches, then clip back any that protrude too far and spoil the tree's outline. If one side is particularly dense, you can selectively shorten a few branches to create a more balanced appearance. Work gradually, as it's easy to remove too much.

    Recent findings suggest that some unevenness comes from the way the tree grew. Christmas trees produce successive tiers of branches as they develop, and the amount of growth between these tiers influences how dense or open the finished tree appears. If one section has widely spaced branches, pruning alone won't necessarily make it look fuller.

    Industry observers note that start by fluffing nearby branches or gently repositioning longer ones to disguise any gaps. You can also fold flexible branches into place and secure them with twine. If one side is woefully sparse, turn the tree so that this side is against the wall.

    Alternatively, you can borrow a branch from a particularly dense area of the tree and use it to fill an obvious gap. Simply cut the branch and secure it to the trunk or a sturdy neighboring branch with green wire, like this Pauleen floral wire from Amazon, positioning it to blend in with the surrounding foliage. Make sure it's firmly attached before adding any decorations.

    According to recent reports, if you'd rather not cut branches from elsewhere on your tree, artificial Christmas tree filler branches or greenery picks can work just as well. Look for ones that closely match the color and texture of your tree's needles, like these Hananona faux pine branches, and tuck them into sparse areas to create a fuller, more balanced appearance.

    Recent findings suggest that you may also be able to disguise a sparse section by trimming back some of the heavier surrounding growth, helping the branches appear more evenly distributed. However, avoid cutting away too much greenery in an attempt to fill a gap – you could end up creating another one.

    Recent findings suggest that the only time you have to worry about a tree’s health is when it is alive. If you have a cut Christmas tree, it is no longer growing. That means that you do not have to worry about its health. Instead, trim the tree to fit well and look nice in your home.

    In a recent development, however, excessive Christmas tree shearing can still affect its appearance and stability. Removing too many lower branches may leave the trunk exposed, while cutting away large sections of the crown can make it difficult to achieve a natural shape.

    Industry observers note that if, however, you buy a living Christmas tree you wish to plant, you do have to worry about keeping the tree healthy. Over-trimming can send the tree into shock or even kill it. The general rule is never to take off more than a quarter of the foliage annually. For most trimmings, stick to 10 percent.

    Don't cut conifers back to the woody inner branches. Most will not sprout latest needles from these branches. Limit your pruning to green, needle-bearing growth. The only exception is if you remove an entire branch back to the trunk.

    If you're growing your own Christmas tree in the garden or keeping a living tree to use again in future years, pruning requires a different approach. Unlike a cut tree, a living evergreen needs to maintain healthy growth and develop a strong, balanced structure.

    Young Christmas trees generally need only light corrective pruning during their first few years. This might involve removing damaged branches, correcting an uneven shape, or dealing with two competing upright shoots. Ideally, the tree should have one dominant central leader to maintain a straight trunk and a natural pointed crown.

    Industry observers note that more regular shaping can begin as the tree becomes established, often around its third growing season. For many Christmas tree species, growers carry out their main shearing once the latest shoots have finished extending but before the fresh growth becomes fully firm. The timing varies according to the species and growing conditions.

    For a living Christmas tree you hope to keep for years, though, it's best to prune conservatively. Focus on correcting problems rather than heavily shearing the entire tree, and always check the pruning requirements of the particular species you're growing.

    It has been revealed that many people get overexcited when they start pruning a Christmas tree and are shocked to find out they have cut off too much. If this is you, take a breath. It’s only a Christmas tree. Resist the temptation to keep cutting elsewhere to even things up. A few strategically placed decorations will usually disguise the problem more effectively than further pruning.

    If you have snipped a few times too many and created a bare spot (or two!), here are a few tips for covering up the damage:.

    As you move through the necessary pruning, you’ll want to keep these few key rules in mind:.

    It has been revealed that on the exterior, the window-seat bump-out lets the house live larger without increasing its footprint. Clad in the same wood as the front entry, the bump-out creates a cohesive and striking connection between the front and back of the house.

    #171779. Want To Befriend A Woodpecker? Here Are 6 Easy Ways To Attract These Striking Birds To Your Yard

    Want To Befriend A Woodpecker? Here Are 6 Easy Ways To Attract These Striking Birds To Your Yard

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (942 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Long tied to forest and earth deities, woodpeckers are some of the most fascinating (and symbolically-laden) birds to welcome into your backyard.
    • That's right, folks; the birth month bird for August babies everywhere, the woodpecker represents curiosity, persistence, and determination.
    • Whether you believe in that or not, though, there's no denying that woodpeckers are considered one of the world's most popular birds for a reason...
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Long tied to forest and earth deities, woodpeckers are some of the most fascinating (and symbolically-laden) birds to welcome into your backyard.

    That's right, folks; the birth month bird for August babies everywhere, the woodpecker represents curiosity, persistence, and determination. (And don't even get us started on what it means if they're the first bird you spot on January 1st!).

    Whether you believe in that or not, though, there's no denying that woodpeckers are considered one of the world's most popular birds for a reason... so, yes, it makes sense you'd like to befriend one!

    Oh sure, they might seem like woodland-only visitors, but there are actually several things you can do to encourage woodpeckers into your yard. In fact, whether you're hoping to spot a great spotted woodpecker, downy woodpecker, or another local species, a few simple changes can make your outdoor space a more welcoming place.

    Suet is one of the easiest foods to use to attract woodpeckers, especially during colder months when birds need extra energy and natural food sources become harder to find. Make sure, though, that you use a sturdy suet feeder designed to allow clinging birds to feed comfortably, and position it somewhere quiet where birds feel safe.

    You should also take care to choose quality suet cakes (you want the kind with seeds or nuts in!) and keep feeders clean. It may take a wee bit of time and patience for woodpeckers to discover your fresh offering, but once they find a reliable food source, they may return regularly.

    Suet isn't the only food worth serving, as woodpeckers also enjoy peanuts and sunflower seeds, particularly black oil sunflower seeds, so long as you pop them in the sort of feeders that allow woodpeckers to perch or cling while feeding. (They don't like it one bit when you scatter food across the ground).

    As ever, we must stress that you should never offer salted or flavored nuts to wildlife.

    According to recent reports, it's all well and good teasing them in, but if you want woodpeckers to stick around, you need to think beyond feeders. And the best way to do this? By planting trees that provide insects, places to forage and shelter in abundance, of course!

    Take care to choose a tree that suits your available space and growing conditions, and remember that even a young tree can contribute to a more wildlife-friendly garden over time. Something like an oak is an excellent long-term habitat investment, while a birch offers lots of opportunities for birds to search for insects.

    It has been revealed that A smaller ornamental tree that offers spring flowers, berries for birds, and beautiful fall color is also a good option for gardens with less room. Something like a serviceberry could work really well!

    Shop Woodpecker-Friendly Trees:.

    Sources indicate that I've said it before and I'll say it again, but a perfectly tidy garden isn't necessarily the most wildlife-friendly one. Dead branches, logs and tree stumps might not be the prettiest to look at (although that's changing; they've been stealing the spotlight at the RHS Chelsea Flower Show across the pond for years) but they can provide valuable habitat for insects and other invertebrates that woodpeckers forage for.

    If you have a dead tree or limb that can safely remain, then, consider leaving it in place rather than removing it automatically. You could also create a small log pile or stumpery in a quiet corner of your yard. As the wood decays, it can add visual interest and become a bug buffet for woodpeckers and other birds.

    If you'd love to attract green woodpeckers in particular, consider giving your lawn a little more freedom, as these birds are particularly fond of ants ; in fact, they love nothing more than to use their long tongues to dig into nests and crevices to sccop them out and gobble them up.

    According to recent reports, avoid pesticides, then, and leave a patch of grass to grow longe if you can. You don't need to abandon lawn care completely, but creating a less manicured patch? It will encourage much more natural wildlife activity.

    It has been revealed that just like other backyard birds, woodpeckers need fresh water for drinking and bathing. A shallow birdbath with gently sloping sides is a must, then, especially during hot weather or when natural water sources freeze.

    Be sure to pop it somewhere relatively quiet, with nearby trees or shrubs where birds can retreat if startled, but without dense cover immediately beside it where predators might lurk. A fine balance to strike, but a vital one, as I'm sure you'll agree.

    Look, attracting woodpeckers isn't about transforming your yard overnight. By providing reliable food, planting trees, preserving natural habitat and offering fresh water, though, you can make your outdoor space a place where wildlife feels welcome. And when that distinctive drumming or flash of color finally catches your eye? Well, then you'll know the effort was all worth it.

    Kayleigh is an enthusiastic (sometimes too enthusiastic!) gardener and has worked in media for over a decade. She previously served as digital editor at Stylist magazine, and has written extensively for Ideal Home, Woman & Home, Homes & Gardens, and a handful of other titles. Kayleigh is passionate about wildlife-friendly gardening, and recently cancelled her weekend aims to build a mini pond when her toddler found a frog living in their water barrel. As such, her garden – designed around the stunning magnolia tree at its centre – is filled to the brim with pollinator-friendly blooms, homemade bird feeders, and old logs for insects to nest in.

    📅 27 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1453 w)

    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    7 Popular Garden Plants That Need Extra TLC Before Winter – Here's How to Protect Them From the Cold

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1453 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that with winter just around the corner, your garden is busy adjusting to the changes in light and temperature and, while some plants won’t fail to return next year, others are more vulnerable and need your help to survive.
    • It has been revealed that some of these garden stalwarts are tender perennials that simply won't survive outdoors in winter, while others are technically hardy but still a little vulnerable, so overwintering these plants well is vital.
    • Dahlias are some of the most varied and prized flowers of a late summer and fall garden, but they’re really only hardy in zones 8 through 11.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that with winter just around the corner, your garden is busy adjusting to the changes in light and temperature and, while some plants won’t fail to return next year, others are more vulnerable and need your help to survive. Many of our favorite flowering plants are the most susceptible to harm from changing temperatures, deep freezes and drying winter winds, so if you want lots of blooms again next year, give them the winter protection they need.

    It has been revealed that some of these garden stalwarts are tender perennials that simply won't survive outdoors in winter, while others are technically hardy but still a little vulnerable, so overwintering these plants well is vital. From protecting shrubs growing in the ground to digging bulbs up to take indoors, here's how to protect plants through winter so they wake up healthy in spring, ready for another bumper season of blooms.

    Dahlias are some of the most varied and prized flowers of a late summer and fall garden, but they’re really only hardy in zones 8 through 11. Their tuberous roots are susceptible to getting mushy in wet conditions and frozen in cold winter ground so leaving them in the ground is risky, especially in zones 6 and colder.

    The best way to protect these plants for flowers next year is to lift dahlia tubers out of the ground after the first deep frost blackens the foliage. Cut the stems back to a couple inches, then carefully dig around and lift out the crown and tubers. Let these dry for a few days to cure and then store dahlia tubers in a box of wood shavings – a compressed bale of natural pet bedding such as this from Amazon is a cheap and convenient way to buy. Keep the box in a cool but frost-free, dry storage area such as an unheated garage, and you'll overwinter dahlias to replant next spring.

    Another plant that benefits from lifting is canna, which is only generally hardy in zones 7 through 10 because it grows from rhizomes that are vulnerable in freezing winter ground. Exact hardiness depends on the variety, so know your type and growing zone.

    Sources indicate that once the foliage has blackened after a frost, cut the stems back to four to six inches (10 to 15 cm) and then carefully dig up canna rhizomes to store for the winter. As with dahlias, it’s best to let these dry for a few days before storing them in a material like wood shavings. Overwinter canna rhizomes in a dark, cool and dry storage area until spring weather has warmed up enough to replant them outdoors.

    One of the most popular hydrangeas for its bright blue or pink flowers, bigleaf hydrangeas, also known as mophead hydrangeas, are typically hardy in zones 5 through 9. However, while the shrubs themselves cope with cold weather just fine, the issue with overwintering hydrangea shrubs that flower on old wood is the potential damage to next year’s flower buds that have developed before winter arrives. A cold snap can damage these buds, reducing the number of flowers you get next summer.

    Sources indicate that to protect hydrangea buds, you’ll need to do more than simply covering the roots zone with mulch. Place four stakes in a square around the shrub and wrap burlap like this from Walmart for protection. In a very cold climate, increase the insulation by filling the space between the burlap and the plant with dry leaves.

    Industry observers note that hybrid tea roses can be hardy from zones 4 through 9, but there is some variation by cultivar, and they're still a little vulnerable to cold weather compared to other types of roses. So, to overwinter roses in a region with a harsh climate, give them some winter protection to ensure they make it through to spring in a healthy state, ready for strong growth.

    Your roses are vulnerable to damage caused by freeze-thaw cycles in the soil and winter damage to canes. First, clean up any plant debris on the ground to reduce the risk of disease, then loosely tie the canes together for extra support in damaging winter winds. Mound soil or compost around the base of the plant and for a final layer of insulation, top with a natural mulch such as Miracle-Gro All Natural Mulch, available from The Home Depot.

    Sources indicate that rosemary is a Mediterranean herb that's generally hardy in zones 8 through 10. The best way to overwinter rosemary in colder climates is to bring it inside: trying to protect this plant outside with mulch is risky as it's very susceptible to wet, cold soil and drying winter winds. However, using a mulch is helpful in zones 7 or 8 to give the roots a little extra insulation.

    According to recent reports, in colder areas, dig up your rosemary plant and move it into a pot that you can bring it indoors. Even better, grow rosemary in a pot year-round as it won’t appreciate being dug out of the ground once established. This Mediterranean herb is one of those plants that grow better in terracotta pots because of the well-drained conditions the porous clay walls create. And because the pot won't be left outside in freezing temperatures, a cheap terracotta planter like this from Lowe's is all you need.

    It has been revealed that rosemary doesn't tolerate soggy roots so to improve drainage, mix perlite like Back to the Roots Organic Perlite, available from Walmart, into any all-purpose potting mix at a ratio of 1:3. Indoors, give your potted plant a cool, bright spot and avoid overwatering.

    Species and varieties of Colocasia and Alocasia offer large, striking, tropical leaves in summer but are only hardy in zones 8 through 11. Elephant ears grow from corms (large underground structures similar to tubers) which should be dug up for winter in colder growing zones.

    Industry observers note that to store Elephant ear corms over winter, let the foliage die back after a frost, then cut back the stems and leaves. Dig around the corm and lift it from the ground, allowing it to dry for up to two weeks before storing in wood shavings in a cool, dry spot. If your Elephant ear is growing in a pot, and small enough, the other option is bring it indoors for winter. While some types can be kept actively growing to enjoy as a houseplant, it's more usual to trim and overwinter tropical plants indoors in a semi-dormant state in a bright but cool spot.

    Many salvias are winter hardy up to zone 3, but in regions with cold winters, more tender varieties are usually grown as annuals. Alternatively, you can try to protect these tender salvia varieties like Brazilian sage or gentian sage from winter weather, and this strategy works best in borderline zones like 6 or 7.

    To overwinter tender salvias outside, use a thick layer of an airy natural mulch such as long-needle pine straw mulch like this from Amazon around the root zone and crown. In a more exposed garden, bark chips like these Pine Mulch Nuggets, also from Amazon, are heavier but create the same airy conditions. Leave the stems in place as they're hollow and trap air that can help insulate the crown.

    If you're growing tender salvias in containers, simply bring them inside for the winter, placing them in a spot with bright light and reduce watering as growth will slow.

    Timing for winter protection depends on the plant and your local climate and weather in your USDA zone. Tender plants should be brought inside before the first frost, but for plants that grow from tubers, rhizomes or corms that need lifting from the ground, wait until after the first deep frost.

    For mostly hardy perennials that simply need a little protection to remain healthy outside, you need to strike a balance between acting before the ground freezes and waiting until the plant goes dormant. Insulating these plants from the cold by mulching or covering too early can delay dormancy and encourage growth that's quickly damaged once temperatures drop.

    According to recent reports, protecting your precious plants before winter arrives isn't complicated or difficult. You simply need to know what you're growing and how the plants tolerate your local winters, then protect them accordingly. A little effort now will reward you next year with strong new growth as soon as temperatures rise in spring, and an abundant display of flowers.

    It has been revealed that mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

    The Best Indoor Garden Systems We've Tested – For Fresh Herbs, Vegetables, and Year-Round Harvests

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2936 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, if you love home cooking, then what could be more appealing than picking fresh herbs and lettuce leaves – or even flavorful cherry tomatoes or chilis – right from your kitchen countertop?
    • Industry observers note that offering features like built-in grow lights, automated watering, and often hydroponic setups, indoor growing systems make it easy to produce fast and surprisingly substantial harvests.
    • In a recent development, with so many systems to choose from, finding the right one for your needs can be confusing.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, if you love home cooking, then what could be more appealing than picking fresh herbs and lettuce leaves – or even flavorful cherry tomatoes or chilis – right from your kitchen countertop? The best indoor garden systems let you grow your own organic produce year-round, even when it’s freezing outside. And unlike a backyard veggie garden, they take up hardly any space: just a small corner near a free power outlet.

    Industry observers note that offering features like built-in grow lights, automated watering, and often hydroponic setups, indoor growing systems make it easy to produce fast and surprisingly substantial harvests. Prices, features, and growing capabilities vary considerably, but most systems are straightforward to use and designed with beginners in mind. Some models have a small footprint, while others offer more capacity for bigger harvests.

    In a recent development, with so many systems to choose from, finding the right one for your needs can be confusing. The Gardening Know How team has tested some of the leading models and shares firsthand experiences with setup, growing performance, maintenance, and harvesting in this guide. We will help you compare the models, identify the features that matter most, and choose the best system for your space, budget, and growing ambitions.

    Here we round up three of the best indoor garden systems. Scroll down to read more detailed reviews from testing each product hands-on. You can also use the links to jump to the indoor garden that interests you the most.

    It has been revealed that if you're new to indoor growing, the Click & Grow Smart Garden 9 is an easy way to get started, ideal for fresh herbs, salad greens, and even dwarf tomatoes. With automatic lighting and self-watering capability, it uses pre-seeded pods, making it easy to get started and delivering great results. Just bear in mind that the replacement seed pods add to the ongoing cost.

    According to recent reports, the Auk Mini combines a compact footprint with a stylish Scandinavian-inspired design, making it ideal for smaller kitchens (especially if you're fond of the IKEA aesthetic). It's exceptionally easy to use, and you can grow your own choice of seeds without buying special pods. With room for just four plants, though, it's better for fresh herbs as opposed to more substantial harvests.

    In a recent development, if you love the idea of enhancing your growing with the latest tech, then the LetPot LPH-Max is the indoor garden for you. This impressive hydroponic system fits a variety of herbs, greens, and vegetables. Its advanced smart features offer plenty of control, but setup can be fiddly for some owners, and some automated functions require extra equipment.

    Industry observers note that drawing on our extensive gardening experience, we evaluated each system for ease of setup and use, build quality, efficiency, crop performance, and overall value for money. Each reviewer tested their indoor garden for at least eight weeks in their own kitchen, assessing everything from initial setup to ongoing maintenance and harvesting. As the systems were tested by different experts in their own homes, growing conditions varied slightly, but all reviewers followed the same assessment criteria.

    From stylish, compact designs to more advanced hydroponic systems, here's how they performed in our kitchens – and who we'd recommend them for.

    Sources indicate that after four months of testing the Click & Grow Smart Garden 9, I can honestly say it's so low-maintenance it feels illegal. Setup took about 10 minutes, including time to read the instructions. Growing tomatoes, lettuce, herbs, and flowers is as easy as loading a coffee pod into a capsule machine: just pop the pre-seeded pods into the reusable grow cups and click them into place. It's completely mess-free, and the built-in grow light means you don't need a sunny windowsill.

    According to recent reports, watering is just as easy. I refill the reservoir about once a week, and the system handles the rest. A handy water-level indicator takes away the guesswork. I even went out of town for two weeks, and my plants kept growing without any care.

    I grew basil, lettuce, dwarf tomatoes, and marjoram. The lettuce grew swiftly and made delicious summer salads, and the basil brought wonderful flavor to my Italian dishes. I was most impressed, though, by the cherry tomatoes. I transplanted a few spare seedlings into standard pots under grow lights, but the Smart Garden tomatoes grew much larger and produced fruit about two months earlier.

    Recent findings suggest that the only disappointment was the marjoram. It sprouted well but barely grew, possibly because the larger basil and tomato plants blocked its light.

    Overall, the Smart Garden 9 has been a really fun, easy, and delicious project. Its sleek design looks great in my kitchen, and I'd highly recommend it to beginners or experienced gardeners looking for a hassle-free way to grow fresh produce year-round.

    Sources indicate that reviewed by Kathleen Walters. Read the full review for more details.

    Industry observers note that the Auk Mini is easily one of the most stylish indoor growing systems I've come across. With its sleek Scandinavian design featuring wooden supports and a choice of black or white finishes, it's a world away from the more clinical-looking hydroponic systems on the market. You can also choose from three base finishes – cork, oak, or walnut – so it's easy to find one that looks at home in your kitchen.

    Setting it up couldn't have been simpler. I just pushed the wooden supports into either side of the base, threaded through the power cable, and attached the adjustable grow light on top. Then it was a case of filling each of the four mini planters with the supplied coco coir and planting the seeds. Mine came with basil and parsley, so I was ready to start growing straight away. Adding the coir was a little messy, and there aren't any convenient pre-seeded pods like you get with some other systems. However, the major advantage is that you can use whatever seeds you like (within reason), rather than being tied to a brand's refills.

    The water reservoir has an indicator that tells you when it's full or needs refilling, and you also get two little bottles of nutrients labeled Grow and Flavor – which felt delightfully Alice in Wonderland! You just pump these into the reservoir as directed. The grow light has different settings and a timer, and I particularly liked being able to position it low over the seedlings, then raise it as the herbs grew taller.

    In a recent development, within six to seven weeks, I was harvesting fresh herbs, which was very pleasing. I also loved how neat and self-contained the whole system was once it was set up. It's attractive enough to leave out on display rather than hide away in a utility room, and it has taken pride of place on my kitchen countertop.

    Industry observers note that the main limitation is its size. With room for just four plants, it's really designed for growing a few fresh herbs rather than producing substantial harvests. But if you want something compact, easy to use, and great-looking, then the Auk Mini is a lovely choice. There's now a newer Mini 2, but the original Mini is still available while stocks last.

    According to recent reports, the LetPot LPH-Max makes it easy to grow plenty of edible plants indoors year-round. With 21 small pods and an alternative tray for two larger plants, you can grow practically a whole garden right in your kitchen. It's mess-free, too – no dirt required. Just fill the tank with water, add plant food, and sow your seeds in the sponge-like pods.

    Recent findings suggest that the system was pretty easy to set up, though it took me about an hour to read the directions and work out how everything fit together. I was genuinely shocked by how well my basil grew in just water and plant food. Hydroponics is kind of amazing!

    However, I did run into a few frustrations. I wanted to try the automatic watering and feeding, but it requires an extra 7-liter reservoir to refill the tank. With a rambunctious cat, limited space, and newly refinished hardwood floors, that wasn't practical, so I used manual mode instead. The top tray didn't fit properly, and I was also disappointed that seeds weren't included.

    Ultimately, I think the LetPot LPH-Max is a good choice for those with hydroponics experience or who enjoy integrating technology into gardening. The app provides helpful growing information and remote controls, though a few features didn't work as expected. For beginners or anyone short on space, I'd recommend starting with a simpler system.

    Reviewed by Laura Walters. Read the full review for more details.

    The AeroGarden Harvest is a compact, beginner-friendly hydroponic system that grows up to six herbs, vegetables, or flowers, with a 20W LED grow light, automatic lighting, and handy reminders for adding water and nutrients.

    The Ahopegarden Hydroponic Growing System has a double-layer design that offers a space-efficient alternative to other countertop gardens, with space for 44 pods.

    The iDOO Hydroponic Growing System packs plenty of features into an affordable countertop garden, including Wi-Fi app control, adjustable LED grow lights, automatic timers, and a built-in fan and water pump, with space to grow up to 12 plants.

    In a recent development, indoor garden systems can make it easy to grow fresh herbs, salad greens, and even vegetables, but there's quite a difference between compact countertop systems and larger, fully automated hydroponic systems. Before buying, think about what you want to grow, how much space you have, and how much time you're willing to spend looking after your plants. These are the main things to consider.

    Recent findings suggest that start by deciding where to position your indoor garden. Countertop systems are ideal for kitchens, but check the dimensions carefully – including the grow light's maximum height. These are often height-adjustable, but not always. You'll need enough clearance for plants to grow, as well as easy access to refill the water reservoir and harvest your crops.

    Recent findings suggest that plant capacity is another important consideration. Smaller systems, such as the four-pot Auk Mini, are ideal for keeping a few fresh herbs on hand, while larger models can grow a wider variety of crops. However, just because an indoor garden has 20 growing positions doesn't mean you can actually grow 20 mature tomato plants. Larger crops like tomatoes need more room for their roots and foliage, so you may need to leave some planting spaces empty. But you can plant several herbs and lettuces as cut-and-come-again crops.

    Recent findings suggest that indoor garden systems are mainly used for herbs and leafy greens, including basil, parsley, lettuce, and arugula. These grow relatively quickly, don't need much space, and can provide repeat harvests.

    However, if you're hoping to grow tomatoes, peppers, or strawberries, you'll need to be more selective. Fruiting crops generally need more lighting, more growing space, and a longer growing period. Look for a system with an adjustable grow light and enough height to accommodate mature plants. Compact or dwarf varieties are usually the best choice.

    In a recent development, many indoor garden systems use hydroponics, meaning plants grow without traditional soil. Instead, their roots receive water with nutrients added using liquid feed, and they are often supported by sponges or another growing medium. These systems can be very efficient, but you'll need to keep the water reservoir topped up and add nutrients regularly.

    Other systems use specially formulated growing media, such as Click & Grow's pre-seeded Smart Soil pods or the coco coir supplied with the Auk Mini. These can be particularly straightforward for beginners.

    Industry observers note that it's also worth checking whether you're restricted to the manufacturer's own seed pods. Some systems require you to buy compatible refills, while others allow you to use your own seeds, giving you more freedom to experiment with different varieties and potentially saving money over time.

    Recent findings suggest that one of the biggest advantages of an indoor garden system is that you don't need a sunny windowsill. Built-in LED grow lights provide all the light the plants need, and most systems include a timer to switch them on and off automatically.

    Sources indicate that look for adjustable light height, particularly if you want to grow anything taller than herbs or lettuce. Some systems also offer different lighting modes for leafy growth and flowering or fruiting crops.

    More advanced models include touchscreen controls, smartphone apps, automatic nutrient dosing, and water-level alerts. These features can be convenient, but they aren't essential for successful growing. A simpler system with reliable lighting and watering is often a better choice if you're new to indoor gardening.

    Sources indicate that although indoor garden systems are low-maintenance, they aren't completely hands-off. You will still need to refill the water reservoir, add liquid fertilizer where required, prune plants, and harvest regularly. Hydroponic systems may also need periodic cleaning to prevent algae buildup and keep pumps and water lines working properly.

    Consider how easy the reservoir is to access and clean, whether the system has a water-level indicator, and how often you'll need to refill it. If you travel frequently, a larger reservoir or automatic watering feature could be particularly useful.

    Indoor garden systems range range from fairly affordable countertop models to high-tech setups costing several hundred dollars or more. However, the initial purchase price isn't the only expense to consider.

    It has been revealed that LED grow lights use electricity, although they're generally more energy-efficient than older lighting technologies. You can check the wattage and daily operating time to estimate running costs.

    Industry observers note that you'll also need to factor in the cost of replacement seed pods, the growing media, nutrients, and potentially other accessories. Proprietary pods can make planting wonderfully convenient, but the costs can add up if you're growing continuously.

    Industry observers note that finally, think about what you actually want from your indoor garden. If your main goal is to save money on groceries, a small system growing a handful of herbs may take a long time to pay for itself. But if you enjoy gardening, want fresh ingredients year-round, or simply love watching things grow, the convenience and enjoyment can make it a worthwhile investment.

    Industry observers note that yes. Indoor garden systems can be a worthwhile investment if you enjoy growing your own food and want a to be harvesting fresh herbs and leaves throughout the year. They're particularly useful if you don't have a garden or want to keep growing through winter. However, they're unlikely to save you a fortune on groceries, especially once you factor in electricity, nutrients, and replacement growing supplies. The real value lies in the convenience, enjoyment, and satisfaction of harvesting your own produce whenever you need it.

    It has been revealed that indoor garden systems are ideal for growing herbs such as basil, parsley, cilantro, mint, and chives, along with leafy greens like lettuce, arugula, spinach, and kale. Some systems can also be used to grow smaller vegetables, including dwarf tomatoes, peppers, and even strawberries. The key is choosing plants that suit the available growing space and lighting. Fast-growing, compact crops tend to give the best results.

    Most small indoor garden systems are inexpensive to run, thanks to energy-efficient LED grow lights. For example, a 20-watt light running for 16 hours a day uses approximately 9.6 kWh of electricity per month. At an electricity rate of $0.17 per kWh, that works out to around $1.63 a month. Larger systems with more powerful lighting, pumps, and automated features will use more electricity.

    Yes, but you'll need the right system and varieties. Compact or dwarf tomatoes are particularly well suited to indoor growing, provided they receive enough light and have room to develop. Strawberries can also grow successfully indoors, although they need sufficient light, nutrients, and pollination to produce fruit. Look for a system with adjustable lighting and enough space for mature plants, and avoid overcrowding.

    Yes. Because hydroponic plants grow without traditional soil, they rely on nutrients dissolved in the water to provide the minerals they need. Most systems come with a starter supply of specially formulated liquid nutrients. Avoid using ordinary garden fertilizer unless the manufacturer specifically recommends it, as it may not contain the right balance of nutrients or dissolve properly. Some systems automate nutrient dosing, while others require you to add it manually.

    Sources indicate that absolutely. In fact, many indoor garden systems are designed specifically for people with little or no gardening experience. Models with pre-seeded pods, automatic grow lights, and self-watering reservoirs take much of the guesswork out of growing plants. The Click & Grow Smart Garden 9 is a particularly beginner-friendly option, while systems such as the Auk Mini offer more flexibility to experiment with your own seeds. Start with easy crops like basil or lettuce, follow the instructions, and you'll soon be enjoying your first homegrown harvest.

She previously served as Editor on Period Living magazine, and worked for Homes & Gardens, Gardening Etc, Real Homes, and Homebuilding & Renovating. Melanie has spent the last few years transforming her own garden, which is constantly evolving as a work in progress. She is also a passionate organic home grower, having experimented with almost every type of vegetable at some point. In her home, Melanie tends to an extensive houseplant collection and is particularly fond of orchids.

    Sources indicate that I first started growing microgreens as something to do during the winter months when my restless green thumb began to feel neglected. What I didn’t expect was just how much I’d enjoy the process – or how rewarding it would be to have a steady supply of fresh, delicious greens right at my fingertips.

    My microgreens fascination began with a little Dollar Tree mini greenhouse I picked up last spring, and honestly, it did the job. It was one of those inexpensive gardening finds that proved you don’t need a fancy setup to get started. As much as I enjoyed my budget setup, though, that dollar-store greenhouse grew brittle and flimsy the more I used it.

    According to recent reports, I started thinking there had to be a better way to grow microgreens by my kitchen window that would make the process easier. I'd seen plenty of clever options among the best indoor garden systems, but I wanted something specifically designed for microgreens. So, I traded my DIY mini greenhouse for the Vego Garden EZ Microgreens Planter – which you can buy directly from Vego or from Amazon at a discounted price for Black Friday – curious to see whether it was actually worth the upgrade...

    According to recent reports, this 7" x 5" mini greenhouse, complete with a waterproof seed-starting tray and clear humidity dome, was where it all began. Most people who bought one were probably planning to start flower or vegetable seeds, but I saw something else: a little tray with a humidity dome that looked perfect for growing a nice harvest of microgreens.

    It has been revealed that and it worked! Well, for a month or so, anyway.

    According to recent reports, there were a few drawbacks. For starters, the tray had no drainage holes, so I had to poke some into the thin plastic myself. That may have compromised its rigidity a little, and I also needed to place a second tray underneath to catch any excess water.

    It has been revealed that my first planting was a success, even using a packet of seeds I'd picked up at the dollar store. But after a few rounds, the plastic started to feel flimsy, and I quickly realized that dealing with soil indoors wasn't something I particularly enjoyed. It was messy, and, from what I'd been reading, you don't actually need soil at all to grow microgreens!

    When my planter set arrived, I was eager to get started! One thing I immediately liked was that it came with not one, but two complete planter dome sets. That means you can grow twice as much or, if you don't need quite so many microgreens, share the second set with a gardening friend.

    The kit also includes four 10" x 10" microgreens trays, two humidity dome covers, and 20 ready-to-use bamboo fiber growing mats. That's enough to grow up to four different varieties of microgreens side by side, which I thought was a lovely bonus. Just imagine having a selection of flavorful, brightly-colored greens ready to harvest!

    In a recent development, if you're concerned about growing food in plastic containers, these planters are made from food-safe plastic, and the natural bamboo fiber growing mats mean you don't need to add soil. It's a simple, tidy way to grow fresh greens right on your kitchen counter.

    Getting everything set up was surprisingly easy, too. The step-by-step instruction booklet was handy, but after just a quick glance, I realized I was probably overthinking things. This was going to be much easier than my first microgreens-growing experiment!

    Recent findings suggest that everything I needed to get started was right in the box. First, I placed the water reservoir on the table, popped in the planting trays, and added the bamboo fiber mats, making sure the little wicking tabs were tucked underneath so they could reach the water below. Then came the fun part: sprinkling the seeds over the mats!

    Once everything was in place, I filled the reservoir to the maximum fill line and gave the seeds a light misting to help settle them.

    According to recent reports, for this first growing round, I chose this pack of Mellow Blend Microgreens seeds from Botanical Interests. I thought this would be a great starter mix, containing broccoli, kohlrabi, red acre cabbage, and more. The greens are on the milder side, which suits my taste, but now that I have this planter, I definitely plan to experiment with some other varieties and blends.

    Sources indicate that and that's really it! No soil, no mess, just seeds, bamboo fiber mats, and water.

    I popped the humidity dome on top, closed the vent to keep the moisture in, and placed the whole setup by my kitchen window alongside my other houseplants. If you don't have a sunny spot available, you can also use a grow light, like Vego's adjustable Grow Lights Stand, which is compatible with the microgreens planter.

    It took about three days before I started seeing little sprouts appear, and in 8 days, I had leaves and a thick mass of roots. It's such a fun process to watch them grow. Microgreens really do seem to spring up before your eyes! The instructions recommend opening the dome vent as soon as you see upcoming growth, so that's exactly what I did.

    One other thing to keep an eye on is the water level. You want to make sure the little wicking tabs on the bamboo mats stay in contact with the water in the reservoir below. That way, your growing microgreens have a steady supply of moisture without you having to fuss over them too much.

    For me, the answer is yes! If you enjoy growing microgreens, this is a nice little investment that makes the whole process easier, tidier, and more enjoyable. It's also a great gift idea for the avid gardener who seems to have everything else.

    I especially like that I can use this planter set year-round. But now that summer is gone and the garden is put away for the winter, having fresh greens growing on my kitchen windowsill gives me the little gardening fix I need.

    It has been revealed that my one small gripe is the water-level viewing window on the reservoir. It's quite dark and tends to cast a shadow, making it difficult to see exactly how much water is left. I've found that shining my phone flashlight against it makes the level much easier to see, or I can simply lift the tray to check, but it's one little design detail I'd love to see improved in future versions.

    After starting with a $1.50 mini greenhouse, I can honestly say the upgrade has been worthwhile. I have a much sturdier, neater setup, plenty of room to experiment with different microgreens, and a fresh supply of tasty greens right when I need them.

    If you're a gardener who isn't quite ready to give up growing just because winter has arrived, I'd say this planter is well worth considering!

    For a simple, low-waste introduction to growing microgreens, the Back to the Roots Microgreens Grow Kit includes organic seeds, expanding coco coir discs, and compostable growing trays, with enough supplies for six harvests of fresh, flavorful greens in as little as seven days.

    A common theme in home design is the idea of blending the architecture with the landscape, allowing the building to sit lightly on the land. You might not expect a 4350-sq.-ft. modern home to be a shining example of how to achieve that goal, but this fresh modern home in Bend, Ore., balances a striking architectural presence with a remarkably light touch on the landscape below.

    Recent findings suggest that the newly introduced building required enough space to house multiple generations, but maximum exposure to the meadow setting and mountain views meant siting the house on a hilltop. To meet both requirements while also only lightly interrupting the land, 40% of the home is set above grade, with a cantilevered great room that appears to float over the ground and that is supported by two special-ordered structural steel beams.

    To further capitalize on the views, the common spaces feature expansive glazing, including a 40-ft. sliding glass wall, while roof overhangs allow the exterior to become part of the interior when large doors are open—while also providing shade and protection from the elements.

    According to recent reports, because the house might accommodate one or two people at some times and upwards of 10 at others, the floor plan is broken up into both large and small common spaces. These include a great room centered around a concrete fireplace designed for larger groups, and a roof deck for more intimate gatherings.

    Industry News: How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1049 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan.
    • I like to create purpose-driven designs.
    • It has been revealed that design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    People often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a plan. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

    I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

    It has been revealed that design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

    Sources indicate that the same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

    According to recent reports, in a fresh garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

    Privacy was one of the big considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

    Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

    I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

    Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

    In a recent development, looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

    Understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

    What a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

    Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

    Industry observers note that growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

    I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from big cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

    Industry observers note that even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build upcoming nests.

    The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

    When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

    • Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota.
    • In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden!
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! I’ve recently gotten a few emails from readers asking about submissions they entered through the website link at the end of every GPOD. Unfortunately, I haven’t received any submissions through the form in quite a while. I’m not sure what the problem is, but hopefully there will be a resolution soon. In the meantime, you can submit your photos and captions through the email linked below instead.

    Today we’re touring Arianne and Micah’s garden in Minneapolis, Minnesota. And while looking through their latest photos, I kept forgetting that I was looking at a garden in the Midwest! Arianne has shared their garden with us before, and I’m excited to see what they’ve been growing this year. Here’s Arianne:.

    In Minneapolis, our growing season may be short, but we squeeze every drop of joy out of our small urban garden! It’s packed with flowers I start from seed—like zinnias, cosmos, statice, strawflower, celosia, and amaranth—along with overwintered dahlias. I love cutting fresh bouquets to gift to friends, family, and coworkers. When we’re not admiring the blooms, my husband is cooking outdoors—making wood-fired pizzas, wok dishes, and hosting family birthday celebrations right in the heart of our cozy yard.

    According to recent reports, arianne packs plenty of interest into the garden along in the front yard and along the curb strip. Plants in this section of the garden include dwarf purple smokebush, threadleaf bluestar (Amsonia hubrichtii, Zones 5–8), boxwood (Buxus cvs., Zones 4–9), lamb’s ear (Stachys byzantina, Zones 4–8), purpleleaf sand cherry (Prunus × cistena, Zones 2–8), coreopsis (Coreopsis cvs., Zones 3–9), alliums (Allium cvs., Zones 3–9), sedum, and artemisia. It’s a great mix of foliage colors and textures even when everything isn’t in bloom.

    I love the placement of the patio and pathway. It’s a really useful design technique for maximizing every square inch of a small garden while still leaving plenty of room for outdoor living.

    Industry observers note that absolutely gorgeous section of the garden! This is where we really start to feel like we’re in the tropics. ‘Mars Madness’ hardy hibiscus (Hibiscus ‘Mars Madness’, Zones 4–9) has all the tropical drama while still being hardy enough for a Minneapolis winter. And it’s hard to miss those giant cannas and the colorful foliage on the coleus. I love all the red blooms too!

    One of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual). So much of the color and interest here comes from foliage!

    There is so much to look at in this section of the garden! Those variegated geranium leaves are striking, and I could go on and on about Arianne’s use of color and texture. The apple tree surrounded by all these ornamentals is an unexpected but lovely touch.

    Recent findings suggest that just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

    Industry observers note that another view of the backyard borders. There are so many plants packed into this garden, you would never believe this is a small urban backyard. And, if my eyes are working correctly, I’d say that’s a clover lawn?!

    Tall conifers create a fantastic privacy screen in this view. The garden really is its own secluded paradise.

    A shady combination of hostas, ‘Banana Boat’ sedge (Carex siderosticha ‘Banana Boat’, Zones 4–9), painted fern, purple shield, coleus, and impatiens.

    In a recent development, zinnias, statice, amaranth, and overwintered dahlias are just some of the blooms that make their way into bouquets for friends, family, and coworkers. So pretty!

    In a recent development, thank you so much for sharing your garden with us again, Arianne! It’s always a treat to see what you and Micah are growing, and I think I could spend hours wandering around this garden and still find something fresh to admire.

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (632 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.
    • My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

    This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

    My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

    My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

    According to recent reports, this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

    In the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

    Recent findings suggest that ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

    Recent findings suggest that sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

    One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

    In a recent development, thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy indicates she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what upcoming plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

    Breaking: Shrubs Steal the Show in Bonnie’s Colorado Garden

    📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (565 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that hi GPOD! Yesterday we enjoyed some beautiful fall color in Nancy’s Massachusetts garden, and today we’re heading west to see what fall looked like in Colorado this year.

    Bonnie took these photos in mid-November after an unusually long fall. While the trees certainly put on a show, Bonnie indicates the shrubs were the real stars this year. Here’s Bonnie:.

    It has been revealed that colorado put on a spectacular fall color display this year. My garden was filled with so many vivid hues that I had to capture them in photos. Some years are more colorful than others, and this was certainly a good one! The standout colors came not from the trees, but from the shrubs.

    Welcome to my fall garden! Just walk through the arch and see the colors beyond. ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) starts in spring with dark burgundy leaves, turns green by late summer, and finishes the season in bright yellow. I love this tree!

    Other stars in my fall garden are the barberries, hydrangeas, dwarf smokebushes (Cotinus coggygria cvs., Zones 4–8), and spireas. Oh, and the Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) in the back turned a lovely red this year.

    Barberry, dwarf smokebush, and spireas in the back make a nice composition.

    Industry observers note that I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

    Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

    I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

    Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

    Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

    Another view from the front yard.

    A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

    Thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

It’s true that the right low-growing plants can add texture and beauty to the bottom layer of your garden, but did you know that many creepers also provide valuable food and habitat for pollinators?

    Recent findings suggest that in fact, some of the earliest blooming plants for pollinators are those spring ground covers that many of us push on past at the nursery. From flowering carpets buzzing with bees to tough, adaptable plants that thrive where turfgrass struggles, we’ll dig into some super cool options for creating a living ground cover that supports pollinators and brings your garden to life.

    In a recent development, thanks for sharing another enhancement from your garden, Connie! And I have to know: What variety of watermelon did your husband grow? It’s huge and oblong! I hope it was delicious. Looking forward to the next update! 🙂.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hi GPOD! Longtime contributor Kielian is back today with another beautiful look at her garden in Hamilton, Montana. We’ve followed this garden through the seasons for years, and GPOD readers may even remember Kielian’s first autumn tour from more than a decade ago. Today she’s sharing what fall looks like on the ranch nearly 17 years into the garden’s evolution.

    Recent findings suggest that in the Bitterroot Valley of Montana, fall imparts her special light and changing colors to the ranch. The gardens are closing in on 17 years of beauty and, interestingly, have decided which design they like the most… on their own.

    My detailed blueprints and drawings of plantings have been changed by Mother Nature, who knows so much more than I do about proper placement. Birds deposit valuable seeds in areas I would never have approved of, and the failure of certain plants to survive makes room for those that forge ahead with gusto. Ahh, autumn, how delightful are your colors and resilience.

    Late October in Montana: The ‘Pee Wee’ oakleaf hydrangeas (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Pee Wee’, Zones 5–9) are showing off, and the ornamental pear tree was not going to be outdone.

    The front garden early in the morning: Shadows enhance the color changes.

    Sources indicate that the back deck was sprinkled with maple-tree graffiti. The linden tree boasted brilliant yellow, and a gorgeous crabapple by the pump house screamed for attention with bright red leaves.

    A smokebush (Cotinus coggygria, Zones 4–8) and aspen tree drip with early morning rain.

    A golden sunset scattered early October rays on quaking aspens (Populus tremuloides, Zones 1–6), enhanced by the Bitterroot Mountains as a backdrop.

    Tessa came running along the path through early November changing leaves.

    Sources indicate that an ornamental pear tree with fading black-eyed Susans in front. Winter is on her way.

    Thanks for sharing another season in your garden with us, Kielian! After seeing this garden in spring, summer, fall, and even covered in snow over the years, it’s hard to pick a favorite season. But that golden sunset over the pond with the Bitterroot Mountains in the distance certainly makes a strong case for fall!
